text: Course two's Instances & Environments lesson told you promotion between instances is deliberate and tracked, never a silent copy, but it left the actual mechanism for later. This lesson is that mechanism: the Update Set.

An Update Set is a container record on the sys_update_set table. While it's active, it collects your customizations as individual rows on a related table, sys_update_xml, so that whole batch of changes can be exported, reviewed, and applied to another instance as one unit, instead of trying to track a dozen separate edits by hand.

What actually gets captured is configuration and metadata, not records. A new or edited Business Rule, with its full script and conditions. A UI Policy controlling which fields show, hide, or become mandatory. An ACL controlling which role gets access to a table or field. A new dictionary field, a changed form layout, a new Script Include. Every one of these redefines how the platform behaves going forward.

Here's the boundary worth being precise about. Create a new Incident, add a user to sys_user, update a Change Request's state from New to Implement -- none of that lands in your current Update Set, no matter which one is active. Update Sets move how the system behaves. They never move the data that behavior acts on.

That boundary isn't an accident. If Update Sets captured data too, promoting one Business Rule to Production could drag along every test Incident and dummy user created in Dev while building it -- exactly the silent, accidental copy ServiceNow's design is built to avoid.

Configuration moves in an Update Set. Data never does. Keep that distinction sharp, because it's the foundation for everything else in this chapter. Next up: the real four-step workflow for creating one, and the single most common beginner mistake that sends changes to the wrong place entirely.
